definition: Paid time off accrued based on length of service and appointment type. Accrual rates and maximum balances vary by employee class. Faculty on academic-year appointments typically do not accrue vacation.
Paid leave for personal illness, medical appointments, or care of an immediate family member. Many states mandate sick leave accrual. Some institutions have sick leave donation/sharing programs.
Paid leave for personal business not covered by other leave categories. Typically limited to 2-3 days per year. May or may not require advance approval.

Leave protected under the Family and Medical Leave Act. Up to 12 weeks of job-protected, unpaid leave per year for qualifying reasons (serious health condition, new child, military family). Runs concurrent with paid leave if available.

Leave for military service under USERRA (Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act). Job-protected with reemployment rights. Many institutions provide differential pay (difference between military and civilian pay).
Paid leave following the death of a family member. Duration typically varies by relationship (3-5 days for immediate family, 1 day for extended family). Definition of 'family' varies by policy.
Leave for serving on a jury or responding to a subpoena. Most institutions provide paid leave for the duration of service. Employee may be required to submit jury fee to the institution.

Extended leave (typically one semester at full pay or one year at half pay) granted to tenured or senior faculty for research, writing, or professional development. Usually available after 6-7 years of service. Requires application and approval.
Leave for birth, adoption, or foster placement of a child. May be paid or unpaid depending on institutional policy. Increasingly offered as a standalone benefit beyond FMLA. Typically 6-12 weeks.
Paid leave directed by the institution, typically during an investigation, restructuring, or emergency. Not initiated by the employee. May be with or without restrictions on campus access.

Leave due to a work-related injury or illness covered under state workers' compensation law. Benefits include medical treatment and wage replacement (typically 2/3 of average weekly wage, subject to state maximums).

Approved leave without pay when paid leave is exhausted or not applicable. Employment relationship maintained but benefits eligibility may be affected. Often requires VP/provost approval beyond a certain duration.
Leave for attending conferences, workshops, certifications, or training. Usually paid with expenses covered by the department or professional development fund.

Resources owned or controlled by the institution with future economic benefit. Includes cash, investments, receivables (student, grants, pledges), prepaid expenses, capital assets (land, buildings, equipment), inventories, and deferred outflows of resources.

Obligations of the institution. Includes accounts payable, accrued payroll, unearned revenue (deferred tuition), bonds payable, capital leases, compensated absences liability, pension liability (GASB 68/75), and deferred inflows of resources.

The residual of assets minus liabilities. GASB uses 'net position' with categories: net investment in capital assets, restricted (expendable and nonexpendable), and unrestricted. FASB uses 'net assets' with categories: without donor restrictions and with donor restrictions.

Inflows of resources. Major categories in higher ed: tuition and fees, state appropriations, federal grants and contracts, auxiliary enterprise revenue, gifts and pledges, investment income, hospital/clinical revenue, and other operating revenue.

Outflows of resources for operations. Classified by function (instruction, research, public service, academic support, student services, institutional support, operation of plant, scholarships/fellowships, auxiliary enterprises, hospital) and by natural classification (salaries, benefits, supplies, travel, equipment, utilities, depreciation).

Movement of funds between fund groups that is not a revenue or expenditure. Includes mandatory transfers (debt service, matching requirements) and non-mandatory transfers (internal allocations, overhead recovery distributions). Must balance — every transfer-out has a corresponding transfer-in.
Application received by the institution
Application is being evaluated by admissions staff or committee
Application is missing required materials (transcripts, test scores, essays, etc.)
Full admission offered
Admission contingent on meeting specified conditions (e.g., final transcript, GPA threshold)
Application was not approved for admission
Applicant placed on a waiting list pending space availability
Decision postponed to a future review cycle (common in early decision/action)
Application cancelled by the institution (e.g., duplicate, fraud)
Applicant voluntarily withdrew their application

Real property owned by the institution, including land improvements that are not depreciable (grading, fill). Land is not depreciated. Includes donated land recorded at fair market value at date of gift.

Structures owned or capital-leased by the institution. Includes academic buildings, residence halls, athletic facilities, hospitals, parking structures. Capitalization threshold varies ($50K-$100K typical). Depreciated over 20-50 years.

Capital improvements that extend the useful life of an existing building (not routine maintenance). Examples: roof replacement, HVAC system, ADA renovations, laboratory renovations. Depreciated over 10-20 years.

Movable assets meeting the capitalization threshold ($5,000 is the most common threshold in higher ed). Includes scientific instruments, computing equipment, vehicles, copiers, specialized machinery. Depreciated over 3-15 years depending on type.
Institutional fleet vehicles: cars, vans, buses, utility vehicles, golf carts. May be owned or leased. Depreciated over 5-10 years. Subject to motor pool or fleet management policies.
Desks, chairs, tables, filing cabinets, shelving, lab benches. Often capitalized only as a group purchase (e.g., furnishing a new building) due to per-item cost below the threshold.

Internally developed or purchased software meeting capitalization criteria. Per GASB 51 (public) or ASC 350-40 (private), includes costs in the application development stage. Cloud computing arrangements may not qualify as capital assets post-ASU 2018-15.

Improvements to leased space made by the institution as tenant. Depreciated over the shorter of the improvement's useful life or the remaining lease term. New lease accounting (GASB 87) affects recognition.

Costs accumulated for assets under construction that have not yet been placed in service. Transferred to the appropriate asset category upon completion. Not depreciated while in CIP. Reported separately on the balance sheet.

Books, periodicals, digital resources, archives, and special collections. Institutions may capitalize (GASB allows either capitalizing or expensing). If capitalized, may be depreciated as a group using a composite method or treated as inexhaustible.

Museum objects, artwork, and historical treasures meeting the definition of a collection under GASB 34 (held for public exhibition, protected, kept unencumbered, proceeds from sale used to acquire other items). May be exempt from capitalization and depreciation if meeting all criteria.

Long-lived capital assets that are normally stationary: roads, bridges, tunnels, drainage systems, water and sewer systems, dams, lighting. Institutions may use the modified approach (maintain/preserve condition level) instead of depreciation per GASB 34.
Asset is in use and being depreciated according to institutional capitalization and depreciation policy. Tagged with a barcode or RFID for inventory tracking.
Asset is not currently in use but remains in institutional inventory. May be available for redeployment to another department. Depreciation continues.
Asset temporarily removed from service for repair or refurbishment. Depreciation continues. If repair cost exceeds a threshold (often 50% of replacement value), may be candidate for disposal.

Asset removed from service and disposed of through approved methods: auction, trade-in, donation, recycling, or destruction. Requires disposal authorization (surplus property process). Net book value written off. Federal grants require sponsor notification for assets over $5,000.
Asset has reached end of useful life and is fully depreciated. Removed from active inventory but record retained for audit trail. Physical asset may still be in use but has no book value.

Asset cannot be located during physical inventory. Triggers investigation and insurance claim if applicable. If government-funded, may require disclosure to the sponsor. Removed from active inventory after investigation.

Asset transferred to another department, campus, or entity. Original department's asset account credited; receiving department debited. If transferred to a different legal entity, may constitute a disposal.

Asset under construction or development that has not yet been placed in service. Costs accumulated in CIP account. Not depreciated until substantially complete and placed in service. Common for building projects and major renovations.
Gift aid that does not need to be repaid (e.g., Pell Grant)
Merit- or criteria-based gift aid that does not need to be repaid
Need-based loan where the government pays interest while student is enrolled
Non-need-based loan where interest accrues from disbursement
Federal loan for parents of dependent undergrads or graduate/professional students
Loan from a private lender, not part of federal programs
Earnings from a federally or institutionally funded part-time employment program
Full or partial waiver of tuition or fees
Financial support for graduate students, typically for research or academic merit
Graduate teaching or research assistantship with stipend and/or tuition remission
An award type not covered by the standard codes
Health insurance coverage for eligible employees and dependents. Institutions typically offer multiple plan options (PPO, HMO, HDHP). State employees may be on a state health plan.
Dental care coverage, often offered as a separate plan from medical. May include preventive, basic, and major services with annual maximums.
Vision care coverage for exams, lenses, and frames. Typically a voluntary, employee-paid benefit.

Employer-provided or voluntary life insurance. Employer-paid basic life is common (1x or 2x salary). Supplemental life available at employee cost. Amounts above $50,000 create imputed income (IRS Section 79).
Income replacement for temporary medical disability, typically covering 60-70% of salary for up to 26 weeks. May be employer-paid or voluntary. Coordinates with sick leave and FMLA.
Income replacement for extended medical disability after short-term benefits exhaust. Typically covers 60% of salary until age 65 or recovery. Often employer-paid for faculty.

Tax-deferred retirement savings plan authorized under IRC Section 403(b) for employees of educational institutions and nonprofits. The higher ed equivalent of a 401(k). Common providers: TIAA, Fidelity, Vanguard.

State or institutional pension plan providing retirement income based on a formula (typically years of service × final average salary × multiplier). Common at public institutions. Mandatory participation in many states.
Supplemental retirement savings plan under IRC Section 457(b), available to governmental and certain nonprofit employees. Allows additional tax-deferred savings beyond 403(b) limits.

Benefit allowing employees (and often spouses/dependents) to take courses at reduced or no cost. Graduate tuition waivers above $5,250 per year are taxable income (IRC Section 127). One of higher ed's most valued benefits.

Tax-advantaged savings account paired with a High Deductible Health Plan (HDHP). Employee and/or employer contributions. Triple tax advantage: deductible contributions, tax-free growth, tax-free qualified withdrawals.
Pre-tax account for healthcare or dependent care expenses. Use-it-or-lose-it rule applies (with limited rollover or grace period). Includes healthcare FSA and dependent care FSA.
Continuation of group health benefits after a qualifying event (termination, reduction in hours). Employer must offer; employee pays full premium plus 2% admin fee. 18-36 month coverage period.

Confidential counseling and referral service for personal and work-related issues. Typically covers mental health, substance abuse, financial counseling, legal assistance. Usually employer-paid, no-cost to employee.

Additional retirement contribution by the institution beyond the base retirement plan, often provided to senior faculty and administrators as a recruitment/retention tool. May vest over a period of years.
Budget is being developed. Units have submitted requests, and the budget office is compiling and reviewing. Not yet authorized for spending.
Budget submitted to the next level of approval (dean, VP, budget committee, board of trustees). Under review and may be revised before final approval.
Budget formally approved by the governing board or authorized body. Establishes legal spending authority for the fiscal year. Published to the ledger as original budget entries.
Budget is in the current fiscal year and available for spending. Transactions are being posted and checked against available budget (in commitment control systems).
Budget temporarily locked — no new spending authorized except for contractual obligations and payroll. Typically imposed during mid-year budget shortfalls or pending reorganization.
Budget period ended. All transactions posted, accruals recorded, fiscal year closed. Budget is now historical. Remaining budget does not carry forward (except for designated carry-forward funds).

Budget has been officially amended after initial approval. A budget revision may increase, decrease, or reallocate authorized spending. Requires documented justification and appropriate approval level.
Ongoing budget allocation that carries forward year-to-year (e.g., salary lines, operating base). Distinguished from one-time or temporary budget allocations.
Budget allocation for a single fiscal year that does not recur. Must be re-requested annually. Examples: equipment purchases, one-time program startup costs, bridge funding.
Primary annual or academic-year salary for the position. For 9-month faculty, this is the academic year (AY) base; for 12-month staff, this is the fiscal year (FY) base.
Compensation calculated per hour worked. Used for non-exempt staff, student workers, temporary employees. Subject to FLSA minimum wage and overtime rules.
Fixed payment for a specific role or responsibility, not tied to hours worked. Examples: department chair stipend, graduate assistant stipend, coaching stipend, program director stipend.

Additional compensation for teaching or duties beyond the standard workload. Faculty teaching above their contractual load (e.g., 4/4 teaching 5/4) receive overload pay, typically calculated per credit hour.

Compensation for 9-month faculty working during summer term. Typically capped at a fraction of base salary (often 2/9 or 3/9 of AY salary). May be funded from grants, instruction, or administrative budgets.
Temporary salary increase for faculty or staff taking on additional administrative duties. Examples: interim dean, accreditation coordinator, assessment director. Removed when duties end.
Temporary pay increase for an individual formally appointed to act in a higher-level position during a vacancy or leave. Governed by institutional acting appointment policy.

Additional compensation for working non-standard shifts (evening, night, weekend). Common for facilities, public safety, dining, and healthcare workers. Typically a percentage of base or flat hourly premium.
Compensation for being available to respond outside normal working hours. Common for IT, facilities, public safety, and residential life staff.
Additional compensation based on years of service. More common at public institutions, especially those under state pay plans. May be a flat amount or percentage per milestone (5, 10, 15 years).

One-time or periodic payment for performance, retention, or market adjustment. Less common in higher ed than private sector but used for hard-to-fill positions, athletic coaches, and senior administrators.
Compensation provided for housing, particularly for university presidents, coaches, or employees required to live on campus (e.g., residence hall directors). May be taxable income.

Parent or family member of a current or former student

Contract is being drafted or assembled from templates. Terms, scope, pricing, and legal provisions under development by the requesting department and/or procurement/legal office.
Draft contract sent to the counterparty (vendor, consultant, partner institution). Terms being negotiated. Multiple redline cycles may occur. Legal counsel reviewing risk provisions.
Negotiation complete; contract routed for internal signature authority. Approval levels determined by contract value and type (procurement, real estate, sponsored program, affiliation agreement).
Approved internally; awaiting counterparty signature to fully execute. Both parties must sign for the contract to be binding.

Fully executed contract in its performance period. Both parties performing obligations. Deliverables and payments being tracked. May include milestones, performance metrics, and reporting requirements.
Contract performance temporarily halted due to dispute, non-performance, force majeure, or administrative hold. Terms of suspension governed by the contract's suspension/termination clause.

Contract has reached its end date without renewal. No further obligations except surviving provisions (indemnification, confidentiality, audit rights). Some contracts auto-renew unless notice given within a specified window.

Contract ended before the natural expiration date, either by mutual agreement (convenience) or due to breach (cause). Termination provisions in the contract govern notice period, final payments, and transition obligations.

Contract extended for an additional period under the same or modified terms. May be an automatic renewal or require affirmative action. Renewal terms should be documented as an amendment or new contract.
Below college-level. Does not count toward degree credit.

700+ level. Doctoral seminars, research, dissertation hours.

Continuing education, professional development, or community courses not carrying academic credit.

Data intended for institutional use only (e.g., enrollment counts, section capacity)
Data protected by regulation or policy (e.g., student PII, grades, financial aid). FERPA-protected data falls here at minimum.
Highly sensitive data requiring strict access controls (e.g., SSN, health records, disciplinary records)
Sub-baccalaureate certificate (less than 1 year or 1-2 years)
Two-year degree (AA, AS, AAS, etc.)
Four-year baccalaureate degree (BA, BS, BFA, etc.)

Online instruction with scheduled real-time meetings (via Zoom, Teams, etc.)
Online instruction with no scheduled meeting times. Students access materials on their own schedule.

Senior institutional officers with significant management responsibilities: president, provost, vice presidents, deans, directors. IPEDS new categories map this to: Management Occupations (SOC 11-0000).

Persons with academic rank (professor, associate professor, assistant professor, instructor, lecturer) whose primary assignment is instruction, research, or public service. Includes tenure-track, tenured, and non-tenure-track faculty reported in IPEDS.

Non-faculty employees in positions requiring a bachelor's degree or higher. Includes advisors, counselors, librarians, IT professionals, accountants, HR specialists, student affairs professionals, coaches, and research staff without faculty rank.

Support staff in office and administrative roles: administrative assistants, office managers, data entry, receptionists, records clerks. Aligns with IPEDS Office and Administrative Support Occupations (SOC 43-0000).

Workers in technical roles typically requiring specialized training or an associate degree: lab technicians, IT support, library paraprofessionals, medical technicians, engineering technicians. Aligns with IPEDS Healthcare Practitioners, Computer/Engineering/Science Technicians.

Workers in trades requiring apprenticeship or vocational training: electricians, plumbers, HVAC technicians, carpenters, painters, groundskeepers. Aligns with IPEDS Construction, Installation/Maintenance/Repair Occupations.

Workers in building maintenance, custodial, food service, public safety, transportation, and similar operational roles. Aligns with IPEDS Service Occupations (SOC 31-0000, 33-0000, 35-0000, 37-0000, 39-0000, 53-0000).
Currently employed and in active pay status. Includes workers on regular schedule, reduced schedule, or modified duties.
Employment record exists but individual is not currently in active pay status. Used for seasonal workers between terms or workers awaiting administrative processing.

Approved absence from duties with employment relationship maintained. Includes FMLA, personal leave, medical leave, military leave, sabbatical. Benefits continuation varies by leave type and institutional policy.
Employment relationship ended, either voluntarily (resignation) or involuntarily (dismissal, layoff, reduction in force). Triggers COBRA notification, final pay requirements, and exit processing.
Employment ended through formal retirement. May trigger retiree benefits (if offered), emeritus consideration (for faculty), and pension/403(b) distribution eligibility.
Employment relationship maintained but worker is temporarily removed from duties, with or without pay. Typically pending investigation or disciplinary action.
Worker is deceased. Triggers survivor benefit processing, final pay to estate, life insurance claim, and tax document generation (W-2 to estate/beneficiary).
Temporary unpaid leave initiated by the institution, typically due to budget constraints. Employment relationship maintained; worker retains benefits eligibility in most cases.
Name purchased or scraped from College Board, ACT, NRCCUA, or other list source. No interaction yet.

Application approved. Admit letter/package sent.

Student withdrew after the drop deadline (typically a 'W' on transcript)

A category not captured above. Document in institution or country-specific profile.
Expense report started but not yet submitted. Employee is adding receipts, coding expenses to chartfields, and calculating mileage or per diem amounts.
Expense report submitted for approval. Routing to the appropriate approver(s) based on institutional travel policy and delegation of authority.
Under review by one or more approvers. May require department head, PI (for grant-funded travel), and/or dean approval depending on dollar amount and funding source.
All required approvals obtained. Routed to accounts payable/travel office for audit and payment processing.

Reimbursement issued to the employee via direct deposit or check. Typically processed within 5-10 business days of final approval. Grant-funded travel may take longer due to additional compliance review.
Report sent back to the submitter due to issues: missing receipts, incorrect account coding, policy violations (exceeded per diem, unauthorized expenses), or missing pre-trip authorization.

Expense report rejected. Common reasons: expense not allowable per policy, insufficient documentation, travel not pre-approved, exceeds budget authority, or retroactive request beyond the submission deadline (typically 30-60 days).

Report flagged for detailed review by the travel office or internal audit. May be random selection, high-dollar threshold, or triggered by anomaly detection. Employee may need to provide additional documentation.

Entry-level teaching appointment, typically requiring a master's degree. Usually non-tenure-track. May be full-time or part-time. Some institutions use this rank for ABD (all but dissertation) candidates.

Teaching-focused appointment, typically non-tenure-track. May be full-time with renewable multi-year contracts. Some institutions have a lecturer promotion track (Lecturer → Senior Lecturer → Principal Lecturer/Teaching Professor).
Promoted teaching-focused rank above Lecturer. Recognizes sustained excellence in teaching and service. May carry additional responsibilities such as curriculum coordination or mentoring.

First rank on the tenure track at most institutions. Typically a 6-year probationary period before tenure review. Expected to develop a research/scholarly agenda, establish a teaching record, and demonstrate service.

Awarded upon successful tenure review (at most institutions, tenure and promotion to Associate are simultaneous). Demonstrates sustained scholarly productivity, teaching effectiveness, and institutional service.

Highest standard rank, awarded upon promotion from Associate Professor. Demonstrates national/international distinction in scholarship, excellence in teaching, and significant service/leadership. No fixed timeline; many remain Associate for career.

Honorary or endowed rank above Professor, recognizing exceptional career achievement. Often carries a named title (e.g., 'University Distinguished Professor,' 'Regents Professor'). May include an endowed salary supplement.
Institutional-level appointment transcending departmental boundaries. Recognizes scholars whose work spans disciplines. Reports to provost rather than a department chair. Rare and prestigious.

Honorary title granted to retired faculty in recognition of distinguished service. Conferred by the governing board on recommendation of the department and provost. Retains certain privileges but is not actively employed.

Non-tenure-track rank for faculty primarily engaged in clinical teaching, supervision, or professional practice. Common in health sciences, law, education, and business. May have its own promotion track (Clinical Assistant → Clinical Associate → Clinical Full).

Non-tenure-track rank for faculty primarily funded by external grants/contracts. Expected to be substantially (often 80-100%) externally funded. May have its own promotion track. Teaching is typically minimal or by choice.

Non-tenure-track rank for individuals with significant professional experience outside academia who bring practitioner expertise to teaching. Common in business, engineering, law, and public policy. Terminal degree not always required.
Temporary appointment (typically 1-2 years) for a faculty member from another institution or a scholar-in-residence. Rank mirrors the visitor's home rank or the level of the appointment.

Employee exempt from FLSA overtime provisions. Must meet both salary threshold ($35,568/year as of 2024 DOL rule, subject to judicial review) and duties test (executive, administrative, professional, computer, or outside sales exemption). Most faculty, administrators, and professional staff are exempt.

Employee entitled to FLSA overtime (1.5x regular rate for hours over 40 per workweek). Must track hours worked. Includes most clerical, technical, skilled trades, and service/maintenance workers. Student workers are typically non-exempt but may be FICA-exempt.

Faculty and instructors meeting the learned professional exemption for teaching. No salary threshold required for bona fide teachers. Primary duty must be teaching, tutoring, instructing, or lecturing.

General operating funds with no externally imposed restrictions on use. Funded primarily by tuition, state appropriations (public), and unrestricted gifts. The institution's primary discretionary resource pool.

Funds restricted by the donor or grantor for a specific purpose or time period. Restriction is satisfied when the purpose is fulfilled or the time period elapses. FASB ASC 958 (private institutions) terminology; GASB uses 'restricted — expendable.'

Funds where the donor has stipulated that the principal must be maintained in perpetuity. Only the investment return (subject to spending policy) may be used, and typically only for the donor's designated purpose. FASB ASC 958 terminology; GASB uses 'restricted — nonexpendable.'

Donor-restricted fund where the corpus is permanently invested and cannot be spent. Income distributed per the institution's spending policy (typically 4-5% of trailing average market value). Subject to UPMIFA (Uniform Prudent Management of Institutional Funds Act).

Funds functioning as endowment at the discretion of the governing board, but without a donor restriction requiring permanent investment. The board may choose to invade the principal. Reported as unrestricted in financial statements.

Funds held by the institution as custodian or fiscal agent for others (student organizations, external groups). The institution has no equity; assets equal liabilities. Common for student activity fees collected and disbursed.
Funds available for student or employee loans. Includes federal revolving loan programs (Perkins — now winding down) and institutional loan programs. Repayments recirculate into the fund.

Funds used for acquisition, renewal, replacement, and retirement of institutional physical plant (buildings, equipment, infrastructure). Includes unexpended plant, renewals and replacements, retirement of indebtedness, and investment in plant sub-funds.

Self-supporting operations that provide goods/services primarily to students, faculty, or staff: housing, dining, bookstore, parking, athletics (at some institutions), student health, recreation. Revenue should cover costs including debt service.

Funds from external sponsors (federal, state, foundation, corporate) for specific research, training, or service activities. Subject to the terms of the award and OMB Uniform Guidance (2 CFR 200). Each award typically has its own fund or project code.

Unrestricted funds that the institution's leadership has internally designated for a specific purpose (e.g., strategic initiative fund, deferred maintenance fund, rainy day reserve). Can be undesignated by the same authority that designated them.

Restricted funds that are expendable for a specific purpose in the current or near-term period. Examples: scholarships restricted by the donor to a specific major, gifts restricted to a specific building project. Distinguished from endowment income which is also restricted but perpetual.

Proposal submitted to the sponsor; award not yet received. Institutional pre-award office has reviewed budget, compliance, and authorized submission. May include pre-award spending authorization if sponsor allows.
Proposal is being reviewed by the funding agency. May involve peer review, panel review, or program officer evaluation. Timeline varies: NSF 6 months, NIH 9-12 months, foundations 2-4 months.
Sponsor intends to fund but terms are being negotiated. Common negotiation points: F&A rate, cost sharing, publication rights, IP ownership, subaward terms, human subjects protocol approval.
Award received, account established, spending authorized. PI can charge allowable costs to the grant account. Subject to periodic reporting (technical and financial) per the award terms.

Award period extended without additional funding. Allows the PI to complete the scope of work with remaining funds. First NCE may be grantee-approved (NIH, NSF); subsequent NCEs require sponsor approval.
Spending temporarily halted by the institution or sponsor. Common reasons: compliance violation, audit finding, IRB/IACUC protocol expiration, PI departure, effort certification delinquency.

Award period ended and all spending completed. Final financial report (FFR/SF-425) and technical report submitted to sponsor. Any unspent funds returned or applied per sponsor policy. Account closed to new charges.

Award has ended but the institution is within the final reporting window (typically 90-120 days). Final invoices, cost transfers, and adjustments being processed. Account open for adjustments only, not new spending.
Award selected for audit by the sponsor, OIG, or as part of the institution's Single Audit (2 CFR 200 Subpart F). Records must be retained and available. May delay account closure.

ID from a previous institution (useful for transfer matching)
National Student Clearinghouse or equivalent ID
Open Researcher and Contributor ID for research/publishing
Credit or non-credit course taken at the institution or elsewhere, often under the tuition waiver benefit. May count toward a degree, certificate, or professional credential.

Structured, interactive training session, typically 2-8 hours. May be offered by HR, the teaching center, IT, or an external provider. Common topics: Banner navigation, budget management, inclusive teaching practices.
Program leading to a professional credential (e.g., PMP, SHRM-CP, CPA continuing education, CITI research ethics). Institution may fund exam fees and preparation materials.

Professional conference attendance, including presentation or attendance. Funded through professional development budgets. Requires travel authorization and post-travel reporting at most institutions.
Online synchronous training session. May be recorded for asynchronous viewing. Increasingly common for compliance training (Title IX, FERPA, cybersecurity awareness).

Asynchronous online learning modules accessed through the LMS or external platform (LinkedIn Learning, Coursera, etc.). Often used for compliance training with completion tracking and certificate generation.
Structured learning occurring during normal work through observation, shadowing, job rotation, or stretch assignments. Typically documented in the performance management system.
Formal or informal pairing of experienced and less-experienced employees for professional growth. May be part of new employee onboarding, leadership development, or faculty development programs.

Required training for regulatory compliance: Title IX, FERPA, GLBA information security, Clery Act, hazardous materials, conflict of interest, responsible conduct of research, driver safety. Non-completion may trigger hold on system access or pay.
Paid every two weeks (26 pay periods per year). Most common for hourly/non-exempt staff in higher education. Creates occasional three-paycheck months.
Paid twice per month, typically on the 1st and 15th or 15th and last day (24 pay periods per year). Common for exempt staff at some institutions.
Paid once per month (12 pay periods per year). Most common for faculty and senior administrators. 9-month faculty may receive pay over 9 or 12 months depending on election.
Paid every week (52 pay periods per year). Less common in higher ed; used at some institutions for temporary and student workers.
Single payment for the full appointment period. Used for some fellowship stipends, one-time consulting arrangements, or athletic bonuses.
Compensation calculated and paid per course taught. Standard for adjunct faculty. Payment schedule varies: lump sum at term start, split across term pay periods, or paid at term end.
Payment request received but not yet approved or scheduled. Awaiting department approval, budget check, or documentation review.
Payment approved through all required authorization levels. Queued for the next payment cycle.
Payment approved and included in an upcoming payment batch. Payment date and method (check, ACH, wire) assigned.
Payment issued to the payee. For checks: printed and mailed/distributed. For ACH/wire: transmitted to the bank. Payment number and date recorded.

Payment cancelled after issuance but before clearing. For checks: stop payment issued. Creates a reversing entry against the original payment. Requires re-issuance if the underlying obligation remains.
Payment request cancelled before issuance. The voucher or payment request is closed. Budget and encumbrance may be released.
Payment returned by the bank (ACH return, uncashed check). Common reasons: incorrect account number, closed account, deceased payee. Triggers re-investigation and re-issuance.
Only a portion of the invoiced amount has been paid. Remaining balance is open. Common for progress payments on contracts, partial shipments on POs, or payment disputes.
Payment approved but intentionally held from disbursement. Reasons: vendor dispute, W-9 not on file, missing tax ID, debarred vendor flag, or 1099 compliance issue.

Performance consistently and significantly exceeds expectations. Demonstrates outstanding contributions, innovation, and impact well beyond the scope of the position. Reserved for truly extraordinary performance (typically no more than 5-10% of workforce).
Performance regularly exceeds the requirements of the position. Delivers high-quality work ahead of schedule, takes on additional responsibilities, and contributes beyond assigned duties.

Performance fully meets the requirements and standards of the position. Consistently delivers quality work, meets deadlines, and fulfills all position responsibilities. This is the expected performance level for a competent employee.

Performance meets some but not all position requirements. Some areas need improvement. Typically triggers a performance improvement plan (PIP) with specific goals, timeline (30-90 days), and support resources.
Performance fails to meet minimum requirements of the position despite prior feedback and support. May trigger formal corrective action, reassignment, or termination process. Must be well-documented.
Performance not formally evaluated for this period. Used for new employees in probationary period, employees on extended leave, or positions where evaluation was deferred.
Used following a performance improvement plan (PIP). Employee has shown measurable progress toward meeting expectations but monitoring continues. PIP may be extended or concluded.
A ~15-week academic term (typically Fall, Spring). Most common in US institutions.
A ~10-week academic term (typically Fall, Winter, Spring, Summer)
A ~13-week term dividing the year into three periods
A sub-term or accelerated term within a semester or quarter
A short-duration term (e.g., May term, Winterim, 8-week session)
A full academic year container (e.g., '2026-2027'). Used for annual financial aid and reporting.
A period type not covered by the standard codes. Document in extensions.
Position is authorized and funded but currently vacant. Available for recruitment or internal transfer.
Position is occupied by an active worker. One position may map to multiple workers if job-shared.
Position exists in the system but hiring is suspended, typically due to budget constraints or hiring freeze. The position's budget may be temporarily redirected.
Position has been permanently eliminated. Budget line removed. Cannot be filled without re-creation through position management approval process.
New position request submitted but not yet approved through governance process. Awaiting budget approval, classification review, and/or provost/VP authorization.
Position used for temporary or student worker appointments where multiple individuals can be appointed against the same position number. Common for adjunct pools, student worker pools.
Prospect identified through screening, referral, or research. Not yet qualified.
Research and initial outreach to determine interest, capacity, and inclination.
Active relationship-building: meetings, events, campus visits, engagement activities.
Formal ask has been made or is imminent.
Post-gift acknowledgment, impact reporting, and continued relationship management.
Constituent is not currently in the moves management pipeline.
PO created but not yet submitted for approval. Requester is finalizing specifications, quantities, vendor selection, and budget coding.

PO submitted and routing through institutional approval workflow. Approval levels determined by dollar amount (e.g., department head up to $5K, dean up to $25K, VP up to $100K, president/board above).
PO approved at all required levels. Budget checked and encumbered. Ready to dispatch to vendor.
PO sent to the vendor. Serves as the institution's contractual commitment to purchase. Includes delivery terms, payment terms, and any special conditions.
Some items on the PO have been received and receipted; others are outstanding. Partial payment may be processed via 3-way match (PO, receipt, invoice).
All items/services on the PO have been received and receipted. Ready for final invoice matching and payment processing.
PO fully received and all invoices paid. Any remaining encumbrance is liquidated (released back to available budget). PO is archived.
PO cancelled before completion. Encumbrance reversed. If any payments were made (partial receipt), the cancellation applies only to the unreceived portion. May require vendor notification.
PO modified after dispatch. Changes may include quantity, price, delivery date, or specifications. Requires approval and may re-trigger budget checking if the total increases.
Requisition created but not yet submitted for approval. Hiring manager is still completing position details, justification, and funding information.
Requisition submitted and awaiting approval through the institutional chain (department head, dean/VP, budget office, HR classification, provost, president — varies by position level).
Requisition approved through all required levels. Ready for posting. HR may need to finalize the job posting language and determine advertising venues.

Position actively advertised and accepting applications. May be posted internally only, externally, or both. Posting duration governed by policy (minimum 5-14 days typical for staff; 30+ days for faculty).

Application review period closed (or ongoing for rolling review). Search committee or hiring manager is conducting phone screens, interviews, reference checks, and campus visits (for faculty and senior positions).
Preferred candidate identified and formal offer letter sent. Awaiting candidate response. May be contingent on background check, degree verification, and/or board approval.
Candidate accepted offer and start date confirmed. Requisition closed. Triggers onboarding workflow (I-9, benefits enrollment, system access provisioning, orientation scheduling).
Requisition withdrawn. Search terminated without a hire. May be due to budget cuts, reorganization, failed search (no suitable candidates), or decision to redefine the position.

Requisition temporarily suspended. Common during budget uncertainty, hiring freezes, or when the search is paused for administrative reasons. Can be reactivated without re-approval at some institutions.

Request submitted to bypass standard search process for a direct appointment (e.g., internal promotion, spousal/partner hire, emergency appointment). Requires EEO/AA office and senior leadership approval.
Student meets all SAP requirements (GPA, pace, maximum timeframe)
Student failed to meet SAP at the end of a payment period. Eligible for aid for one more period without appeal.
Student failed SAP, appealed successfully, and is on a monitored academic plan. Eligible for aid while on plan.
Student is ineligible for federal financial aid due to failure to meet SAP requirements
SAP appeal approved. Student placed on probation with an academic plan.
SAP has not been evaluated for this period (e.g., first term)
Person has expressed interest but has not applied
Person has submitted an application for admission
Application accepted; student has not yet enrolled
Student is actively registered in courses for a current or future term
Student has an approved leave and intends to return
Student has voluntarily or administratively separated from the institution
Student has been conferred a degree, certificate, or credential
Student is deceased. Record retained for historical and compliance purposes.
Entering college for the first time (no prior postsecondary enrollment). IPEDS: First-time, first-year.
Entering with credits from another postsecondary institution
Previously enrolled at this institution, returning after a break in enrollment
Currently enrolled, returning for the next term without a break
High school student simultaneously enrolled in college courses
Enrolled at another institution but taking courses here temporarily
Taking courses without pursuing a degree or credential
Has a bachelor's degree, taking additional undergraduate courses
Enrolled solely to audit courses without credit

Faculty member on the tenure track who has not yet undergone tenure review. Typically in a 6-year probationary period with annual reviews and a mid-probationary (third-year) review. Clock extensions may be granted for qualifying life events.

Faculty member who has been granted tenure following successful review. Provides protection against termination without cause (financial exigency, program discontinuance, or adequate cause with due process). The cornerstone of academic freedom.

Faculty member in a position not eligible for tenure. Includes lecturers, clinical faculty, research faculty, professors of practice, and adjuncts. Appointments may be single-year, multi-year, or rolling. Increasingly the majority of faculty in US higher education.
Faculty member whose tenure application was not approved. Typically results in a terminal-year appointment (one additional year). Denial decisions may be appealed through faculty grievance processes.

Tenure removed through formal proceedings for adequate cause (e.g., professional misconduct, research fraud, dereliction of duty). Requires due process consistent with AAUP guidelines and institutional policy. Extremely rare.
Standard journal entry created by accounting staff to record transactions not captured by subsidiary systems (payroll, AP, AR). Requires balancing debits and credits with supporting documentation.
Automatic journal entry generated by a subsidiary system (payroll, accounts payable, billing, grants). Posted through batch or real-time integration. Represents the majority of GL activity.
Entry to correct an error, reclassify an expense, or adjust an estimate. Requires explanation/justification and typically additional approval. Common at month-end and year-end.
Entry to recognize revenue earned or expenses incurred but not yet recorded in cash basis. Examples: unbilled grant revenue, accrued payroll, accrued vacation liability. Required for GAAP compliance.
Entry that exactly reverses a previous entry, typically an accrual from the prior period. May be automatic (auto-reverse flag) or manual. Posted at the start of the new period.
Year-end entry to close revenue and expenditure accounts to fund balance. In fund accounting, closes each fund separately. Prepares the ledger for the new fiscal year.

Entry to move amounts between chartfield combinations (accounts, departments, funds, programs) without changing the net financial position. Common for correcting coding errors or reallocating shared costs.

Entry to eliminate intra-entity transactions in consolidated financial statements. Used when the institution has component units (foundations, hospital, research corporations) that must be consolidated per GASB standards.
Non-monetary entry recording statistical data (headcount, square footage, FTE) in the ledger for allocation and reporting purposes. Does not affect financial balances.

Entry to record the original budget, budget modifications, or encumbrances. In commitment control systems (PeopleSoft), budget entries establish spending authority against which transactions are checked.

Entry to reserve budget for a committed future expenditure (purchase order, contract, salary commitment). Reduces available budget without recording an actual expense. Liquidated when the actual expense posts.
Former member of the armed forces who has been discharged
Currently serving in the armed forces
Member of a reserve component or National Guard
Dependent or spouse of a service member, eligible for benefits (e.g., Chapter 35, MyCAA)
Permanent employee on the institutional payroll with benefits eligibility. Includes both full-time and part-time regular appointments.
Employee hired for a defined period, typically not to exceed 12 months. May or may not be benefits-eligible depending on FTE and institutional policy.
Individual engaged through a staffing agency or third-party arrangement. Not on the institutional payroll; paid through accounts payable.
Individual providing services under a contract (1099). Must meet IRS independent contractor tests. Not an employee for benefits, tax withholding, or FLSA purposes.

Currently enrolled student employed by the institution. Includes Federal Work-Study (FWS), institutional employment, and hourly student positions. Typically exempt from FICA if enrolled half-time or more.

Graduate student holding a funded assistantship (GA, TA, RA). Typically receives tuition remission plus stipend. May be classified as student or employee depending on state law and collective bargaining status.

Individual in a structured learning experience, paid or unpaid. Unpaid internships at for-profit entities must meet DOL primary beneficiary test; universities have more flexibility under educational exception.

Individual receiving a fellowship (external or institutional) for research or scholarly activity. May not have an employment relationship; fellowship stipends are often non-compensatory and reported on 1099-MISC or 1042-S.
Individual providing services without expectation of compensation. Must meet FLSA volunteer criteria. Cannot volunteer in roles identical to their paid position at the same institution.
Retired faculty or staff member granted emeritus status by the governing board. May retain certain privileges (email, library, office) but is not actively employed or compensated unless rehired.
Individual holding a doctoral degree engaged in supervised research training. Classified as employee or trainee depending on funding source (NIH NRSA = trainee, institutional funds = employee).

Part-time faculty hired on a per-course or per-term basis without tenure eligibility. Typically compensated per credit hour or per course. May be subject to ACA hour tracking for benefits eligibility.
